turn_text: Right. Time is going to be out of the essence. And let's hope that if this happens, it's just a brief side show that does not distract the legislature from the really important business at hand, basically handling the entire COVID response. of the state in the three days while also passing a budget that also needs to respond to the pandemic. And so, as you said, Jim, there's huge work to be done here and very little time for petty distractions that are very politicized as regards to this whole face mask issue.

David, I did want to jump in here real quick about the budget per se. We had one of our local lawmakers talking about the fact that the budget might be better off to be after May 31st, given the fact that we still don't know what the federal government is going to help out with. David, is that going to play a factor in how they put this budget together next three days in your opinion?

I think that's a great question. We've gone through periods where there was no budget for a while. We saw that on a Bruce router for more than 18 months. It did a lot of damage to the state to have it last that long. But one can fairly ask the question as to whether passing the budget could wait until a special session held a little bit later this in very early this summer. There's the last couple days that talk has been circulating a lot more and it could well happen because there's so much uncertainty about exactly how much money will be coming from the federal government and under what terms and it's very important to know that because that can make a big difference in an expected $7.4 billion deficit that the state is facing right now.

You know, and the deadline of May 31st is only for passing a budget with a regular majority, you need a super majority after that, but the new fiscal year doesn't start until July 1. So there is certainly time to address some of this. The biggest challenge, it seems to me, David, and maybe you've heard some things differently up in the Chicago area. We have put the question here to the governor, to lawmakers in both parties with, as you said, that multi-billion dollar revenue shortfall. Where is this budget going to be cut? Because we're clearly not going to find the revenue to fill that kind of a gap. There's going to have to be cuts. I've yet really defined a single person who has said where they are willing to cut the budget. They've talked about areas they want to protect. I haven't heard anybody say, here's where I think we should cut. I don't know how we're gonna put a budget together unless people are willing to finally face the reality here that yes, some things are gonna have to get cut pretty dramatically.

Well, $7.4 billion is not an easy hole to fill. And you're right, the politicians have been very circumspect mainly because nobody likes to walk around talking about cuts that may not actually happen. That tends to happen in small groups among the leaders and not really among the rank and file that the real decision-making that happens. And there are no easy targets, obviously. It's interesting to look at, say, some of the things that are threatened, for example, Governor Pritzker has indicated that funding for schools might be caught if he doesn't get his progressive tax. Would that possibly indicate that he sees some fat in the budget for schooling? I doubt it, but he has indicated he's willing to cut if he doesn't get progressive tax. So we'll see over the next few days, or maybe if they decide to wait for a special session sometime in the next few weeks.

We want to come back and talk about the progressive income tax proposal in just a moment. We need to address all any sort of health care issues that are out there because that's the most pressing issue, social issue of our time.
